title: 3D model to Character | 10 Step Process
author: amirati91
selftext:
Last time, we moved from a 2D drawing to a 3D model, along with all the checks we perform before it can pass through the next "gate" (is here, in case you dind't read and have interest: https://www.reddit.com/r/aigamedev/comments/1xsscmk/character\_creation\_process\_from\_2d\_to\_3d/) , which is this stage: walking, running, speaking, and reacting within the game engine.

In my point of view, what separates "AI slop" from well-executed work, even when you lack prior experience as a 3D modeler, animator, or anything of the sort, is attention to detail and standards. And creating a process serves precisely those who do not want to be interned by their own standards.

The ten steps are always in the same order, and the same for every character.

Two kinds of gates: A measured gate is a number that must pass, or the script stops. A human gate is a person who must look before anything moves on. This is especially true with characters in new formats, so it's always important to work with character families, it saves a lot of work.

To generate 3D models, I use Tripo. They create an image, using GPT-2.5 or Midjourney (the latter is great for environments or instances where strict adherence to the prompt isn't critical), and then produce a "smart quad" mesh. I aim for around 15,000 quads, though it often ends up being a bit higher, so I usually generate four options (all for the same credit cost).

Keep in mind that the quad count significantly impacts performance and the number of characters that can be displayed on screen. Greater complexity and detail require more quads to maintain fidelity—and more quads mean more detail, but also a heavier model. I used to perform mesh reduction in Blender (with help from Claude), but it’s not worth the effort; getting the right mesh directly from Tripo saves me hours of work and a significant number of tokens.

**Step 1**

Prepare and mark. Scale, floor, six landmarks. On this model five of the six automatic landmarks were wrong: the puffy sleeves read as skin and the hair hid the chin. One photo is enough to catch that. This character is an interesting subject of study because she has wide hips, which creates optimization challenges as well as an opportunity to improve the process.  


**Step 2**

Examine the body. Sleeves, hips, hair, measured against the characters that came before. Problems are found before the rig, not after it breaks.

![img](ryz8ii44w12i1)

**Step 3**

Rough rig. A posable skeleton in minutes, to judge the body in real poses. Squatting down and raising your arms tends to reveal a number of flaws. This outfit is quite form-fitting, so it’s not an issue; however, looser clothing or garments made of certain fabrics usually require extra attention.

![img](95b9j693y12i1)

**Step 4**

Fingers. Knuckles found from the mesh itself.

![video](ygi5mehuy12i1)

**Step 5**

Loose parts. Tunic and hair get short bone chains (12 and 6 of them) and a spring. For the tunic we learned from Tripo's auto-rig: it weights the cloth to the thigh on its own side, smoothly, with just two bones per point, so the hem barely stretches or folds when she walks. We copied that as the base and left the chains only a small share near the hem, for the swing.

**Step 6**

Hand. Skin weights, one control that closes the fist, eight test poses. 

Most of you likely know this, but Claude doesn’t perceive motion; it processes things frame by frame. Therefore, providing an image of a hand closing, along with a clear, detailed explanation, works much better than trying to get it to "see" the movement through words alone. Keeping this in mind is essential when animating something like a hand closing or a sword fight.

![video](fddw0g02022i1)

![img](4vpkrlb3022i1)

Step 7

Game skeleton. Only the bones that deform. The walk is borrowed from another character on the same skeleton, and fitted: copied as is, her ankles walked 33.5 cm apart, wider than her hips. Fitted, 23.4 cm, the same as standing.

![img](mm8vfirl022i1)

**step 8**

The face is drawn, not sculpted: the 2D expression sheet is split into layers by script (iris, eye white, lashes, brows, mouth) and laid over a smooth 3D face. Five controls drive it, and gaze and speech work on top of any expression.

![video](smv58r45322i1)

Step 9

One file. Rig, final mesh and face controls together.

![video](gcmc3lq6322i1)

Step 10

And once a character has gone through the ten steps, it can do more than just walk. In that example, it picks up a loaf of bread from a table: the body's movement is derived from a text prompt, and the point of contact is calculated—so the hand stops at the object, and the fingers close until they make contact with the surface. 

This works for picking up a loaf of bread, and it also works for a sword fight (though that’s still being tested); the underlying logic is similar, but that’s a topic for a bit later.



![video](znjxvijt222i1)



What we learned: check every automatic guess on a photo. Measure the body before the rig. **Borrowed motion must be fitted, not copied.** When a character breaks a tool, fix the tool, so the next character goes through the same commands. And read the auto-rig before replacing it: its cloth weights were better than ours, and now they are ours too.

replies.author: amirati91
replies.body:
You have every right to be blind.

One-click doesn't move the hair, the hands, or the fingers; the arms pass right through the waist; there’s no expression; the character walks in a straight line, completely devoid of any sway or rhythm. This type of walk is produced by default, before adding any personality to the movement, but even in this raw state, it provides a foundation you can work with.

That wasn't nearly as simple when I first started this project months ago, and it might still not be simple for many others who are starting their projects

replies.author: amirati91
replies.body:
Thanks for reading!

Yes, using AI to animate anything more specific, especially for a character that doesn’t fit into standard Mixamo or "humanoid" bone structures, has been a challenge; I’ve noticed that many others are facing the same issue.

So, I think detailing the process might help someone take a specific part of it, like the rigging, the hands, or the facial expressions, and use that to unblock a piece of their own project. As for the haters, I don’t know what the community gains by spewing garbage on a post meant to share a process, but that’s just how things are.
